articles.title: This company just put the air in Apple’s MacBook Air
articles.summary: Frore Systems put three of its AirJet Mini into a 15-inch M2 MacBook Air and let us put that system head-to-head with a stock M2 MacBook Air. The results were intriguing.
articles.body: Two Fridays ago, I drove down to a squat single-story Silicon Valley office building to see a MacBook Air. There was no security guard, no need to badge in, not even a PR person in my demo room. That’s because I wasn’t visiting Apple headquarters for an unannounced laptop. Instead, I went to San Jose to see an existing MacBook — one surgically modified to prove how far an exotic cooling tech has come. Frore Systems is a startup with $116 million in funding, and I’ve shown you its first product before: the AirJet Mini is a piezoelectric cooling chip that weighs just nine grams and is thinner than two US quarters stacked together. Each nominally consumes one watt and can remove 4.25 additional watts of heat. Here’s the question: what would happen if Frore used those AirJets to cool a laptop that normally doesn’t have a fan at all? What the company discovered — and I saw firsthand — is that Apple’s M2 chip can run faster, for longer, with Frore’s tech on board. Without it, a 15-inch M2 MacBook Air was like a runner that can’t sprint indefinitely without running out of breath. But with three AirJet Minis, the same laptop got a permanent second wind. [Media: Here’s the bottom line: the longer I ran an intensive benchmark on Frore’s modified and unmodified pair of 15-inch MacBook Airs, the bigger a difference I saw. Even during the very first of a multi-minute benchmark like Cinebench R23 or Shadow of the Tomb Raider, the AirJet version pulled out slightly ahead, though perhaps within the margin of error at, say, 29 frames per second with AirJet versus 28 frames per second without. The Xcode benchmark finished in 172.7 seconds with AirJet versus 178.2 seconds without the first time around. [Image: Three AirJet Minis and a custom heatsink inside a 15-inch M2 MacBook Pro. [Image: The reverse of that heatsink — the AirJets strongly suck air through a stack of copper fins atop a custom heat spreader that screws down onto Apple’s logic board. But after half an hour of back-to-back Shadow of the Tomb Raider gaming benches, scores had dipped to an unplayable 22fps on the stock Mac versus 27fps on the AirJet version. I started to see massive stutter on the stock Mac at the 40-minute mark — while Frore’s AirJets just kept breezing on. With Cinebench R23, multicore scores seriously dipped after just a few repeat benches — from 8775 with AirJet to 8380 without. According to a Frore-provided overlay that I watched like a hawk, the stock Mac simply wasn’t able to maintain the same CPU clocks. Both clock speed and wattage plummeted on occasion, presumably because a fanless computer has no other good way to cool itself. What’s happening here is fairly well understood: today’s processors are only as fast as they can be cooled, with many advertising “turbo” modes that the thinnest computers can only maintain for a short time. For example: Apple’s Air can run the M2 chip at 3.2GHz but throttles down to 2.8GHz after 30 minutes of Cinebench R23, says Frore. [Image: A chart from Frore showing how the Apple M2’s megahertz and processor power can take a dive during sustained tasks. But as neat as it was to see the AirJets give Apple’s M2 a second wind, I also walked away a tad underwhelmed. Tomb Raider stutter aside, we’re mostly talking about an already capable computer simply taking a bit longer to perform the most intensive tasks, with less demanding benchmarks (like single-core Cinebench, where I saw identical scores) not stressing the chip enough to make a real difference. More importantly, we already know what Apple’s M2 chip can do when you add airflow — it’s called a 13-inch MacBook Pro! As I reported a few years ago (back when I could ethically cover Apple products), the biggest difference between the 13-inch MacBook Pro and the 13-inch MacBook Air is literally a fan. Since then, we’ve clearly seen in our own M2 MacBook Air and MacBook Pro benchmarks that performance tends to deteriorate over 30 minutes without that fan on board. Frore knows this and brought a 13-inch M2 MacBook Pro for me to test alongside the Airs — but it’s not really an apples-to-apples test if I’m comparing them to a 15-inch MacBook Air with a wider chassis and more thermal headroom. Even so, Frore’s modified 15-inch Air was mostly neck and neck with the 13-inch Pro, rather than regularly beating it. (The Pro did take four seconds longer to complete a run of Xcode.) [Image: Frore carved out a little extra space in the 15-inch MacBook Air’s lid. But there is one good reason Frore picked the 15-inch MacBook Air — at 0.45 inches (11.5mm) thick, it’s one of the thinnest laptops ever made. It’s not clear Apple could fit the fan from its 13-inch MacBook Pro in there — or any fan, for that matter. Even Frore had to painstakingly mill 0.3mm out of the laptop’s lid to give the AirJets a big enough air gap to do their thing, and the company wound up removing the speakers, Wi-Fi antenna, and even the Mac’s internal keyboard connector along the way. But Frore did it, and engineering chief Prabhu Sathyamurthy tells me laptops can get even thinner if they’re designed with AirJet in mind — they could reach 9.5mm in thickness simply by substituting a thinner keyboard and a thin OLED display, the company claims. [Image: Click to enhance and maybe make those numbers large enough to read. There is one thing I didn’t see accounted for in Frore’s proposal, though, and didn’t get to satisfactorily test at Frore’s offices: the all-important battery. While Frore says each of its AirJet Mini chips require one watt of power, I saw three of them consume over five watts from the MacBook’s USB-C port, and the AirJet-equipped MacBook Air (obviously) drained far faster than the power-throttled fanless one did during my tests. Mind you, Frore’s been clear since the beginning that its chips need to be integrated into a device for them to work optimally, and the MacBook demo is anything but where power is concerned. Sathyamurthy says you can expect the AirJet part of a complete system to draw as little as 0.1W or 0.2W when idle, with the AirJet Minis themselves staying turned off until or unless they need to blow. He thinks the average user will see them kick on 10 to 15 percent of the time and not at all for “emails and web surfing.” We’re talking a Zoom call or worse. [Image: For demo purposes only: a USB-C power cable for the AirJets where the MacBook’s speaker used to be. And when they do blow, they blow far quieter than a fan, I can confirm. I had to bend down next to the laptop to hear them at all. The modified laptop also seems a tad cooler than Apple’s fanless MacBook Air — a thermal camera showed me a wider, cooler region instead of a hotspot near the chip. I can’t say this demo convinced me that Frore can make the fan obsolete. I mostly saw it meeting the performance of a fan, with less noise in a tighter space. But that could mean a lot to the right company trying to push the envelope in portability or — pretty please! — using those space savings for additional batteries. I wonder if any laptop manufacturer will give it a go. So far, Frore’s only confirmed design win is this Zotac mini-PC that’ll always be plugged into a wall, but it has prototyped 4K webcams, doorbell cameras, LED light bulbs, and more. Sabrent, Phison, and OWC tried experimental AirJet-cooled SSDs. Frore seems to think AirJets could fit into a Steam Deck, too. I’d love to try a battery-powered system where we can fully see the AirJet way is better. And I’ll let you know as soon as I do. Frore says the AirJet Mini is in mass production now, with larger and smaller versions in development. [Media: Correction: Cinebench isn’t a video rendering benchmark as I originally wrote, but rather a 3D rendering one. I regret the error.

articles.title: The newest Samsung SmartThings hub ditches Z-Wave
articles.summary: Wave goodbye to Z-Wave.
articles.body: Aeotec announced its Smart Home Hub 2 at the IFA tech show this week, marking the end of an era. The hub, produced in partnership with Samsung, is the fourth generation to support the SmartThings home automation platform, and the first without a Z-Wave radio. The Smart Home Hub 2 has twice the performance of its predecessor, according to a press release from Aeotec, and features upgraded hardware, USB expandability, and support for Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee, Thread, and Matter Controller capabilities for SmartThings. Aeotec says it’s built for local-first communications, allowing most automations to run on the hub, so they’ll keep working even if the internet is down. It’s slated to launch in Q4 of 2025. SmartThings users who want to keep using Z-Wave in their home will have to stick with the SmartThings V3 hub (also known as the Aeotec Smart Home Hub). Aeotec plans to discontinue V3 at the end of 2026, but says it just finished a final production run and has plenty of inventory available. Samsung moved away from manufacturing its own dedicated hardware hub a few years ago, outsourcing it to Aeotec. In the meantime, it started to integrate SmartThings Hubs with Matter and Thread support into its TVs, soundbars, and other appliances. However, a dedicated hub like the SmartHome Hub 2 is more powerful, can handle a greater number of devices, offer more local automations, and has a better range, which makes it a better choice for bigger smart home setups. Aeotec’s hub was also the only choice if you wanted to run Z-Wave devices in your SmartThings home. But it looks like those days are nearly over.

articles.title: Insta360’s Luna Ultra 8K stabilized camera is now available in the US
articles.summary: Insta360’s 8K Luna Ultra stabilized camera is now available in the US for $770 and features a detachable touchscreen remote that can livestream video.
articles.body: Following months of teases, leaks, a secretive debut at NAB 2026, and an initial launch in China, Insta360 finally announced global availability for its first handheld stabilized camera. The Luna Ultra features a pair of 8K cameras atop a 3-axis gimbal, offering an upgrade to DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4 and Pocket 4P, which both max out at capturing 4K footage. While the latest versions of DJI’s baby steadicams still aren’t sold in the US, the new Luna Ultra is available starting today for $769.99 through Insta360’s online store and other retailers including Amazon, B&H, and Best Buy. The Luna Ultra’s primary camera features a 1-inch 8K sensor paired with a Leica Summicron lens while its secondary camera uses a smaller 1/1.3-inch sensor with a telephoto lens offering up to 12X zoom capabilities, or 6X lossless. Still images are captured at up to 37-megapixels, but like Insta360’s Ace Pro 2 action camera, 8K video captures max out at 30fps. Dolby Vision, 10-bit I-Log, and additional color profiles developed by Leica are supported when capturing 8K video, as well as several cinematic filters that can be applied in-camera, but bumping the frame rate to 60fps requires a drop in resolution to 4K. You can boost the 4K frame rate to up to 120fps for capturing slow-motion footage, but doubling that to 240fps limits the Luna Ultra’s resolution to 1080P. [Image: The Luna Ultra’s controls and 2-inch OLED touchscreen can be removed and used as a wireless remote with previews over 65 feet away. DJI Osmo Pocket users will be familiar with the Luna Ultra’s design, including its 2-inch rotating OLED touchscreen and a built-in microphone that can be augmented by connecting other Insta360 wireless mics. What sets the Luna Ultra apart from DJI’s Pocket cameras is that its touchscreen and controls can be detached and used as a wireless remote with a livestreamed preview at a distance of over 65 feet. That alone could make it a tempting alternative to vloggers working without a dedicated camera operator. Insta360 estimates the Luna Ultra’s 1,550mAh battery will power the camera for up to four hours between charges, but that will depend on what features are used and how hard its stabilization system has to work. The camera features the company’s Deep Track 5.0 technology that can automatically track individual subjects or groups and zoom in and out to ensure they remain properly framed. [Image: Some of the Luna Ultra’s accessories include tiny tripod legs providing a more stable base for the camera when standing on its own. Optional accessories include a POV Head Tracker worn over the ear that translates your head movements to the cameras so they’re always looking where you are, a battery-boosting handle, ND filters, and a wide-angle lens. You can also expand the Luna Ultra’s storage to up to 1TB with a microSD card, but out of the box you get 47GB built-in. The Verge’s Sean Hollister has been testing the Insta360 Luna Ultra for the past few weeks and has a full review enroute. Due to the camera’s release date being unexpectedly pushed up, he shared some initial thoughts on its performance, hardware, and new features: [Image: The Verge’s Sean Hollister was able to zoom in on the sheet music during a piano recital using the Luna Utra’s telephoto lens. > So far, I don’t think I actually prefer the Luna Ultra to my Osmo Pocket 3! The second lens with 6x lossless zoom and wireless detachable touchscreen are very nice to have, letting me capture my daughter’s ballet recital and my dad’s wedding ceremony without leaving my seat. I could read the notes at my kid’s piano lesson from across the room at 12x zoom unlike the DJI. > But the Luna’s nowhere near as effortless to use. It’s not as compact and easy to grip, it’s so dang annoying to have to un-navigate a menu after you change each setting (you can’t just hit record to go back to recording mode), and most importantly, it’s even harder to tell if things are in focus on the Luna than my DJI. I’d rather have a sharper screen than a detachable one, particularly since the Luna isn’t quite as good at automatically choosing the right focus to begin with. I can generally trust the Pocket 3, but the Luna needs some more work. > I am finding the Luna slightly better at automatically tracking people, and the 47GB of built-in storage means no swearing when I leave the SD card in my PC. It’s clever how the extended grips include tiny fold-out tripods, too, and I’m looking forward to trying other useful accessories like a neckmount and an earpiece that rotates the camera to match your real head’s point of view.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Criança de 1 ano engole bateria de lítio e é internada no Acre | G1
articles.standfirst: Criança deu entrada no Pronto-Socorro de Rio Branco nessa quinta-feira (3) e o objeto foi retirado na manhã desta sexta (4) por meio de uma endoscopia. Paciente segue em observação na unidade de saúde.
articles.summary: Criança deu entrada no Pronto-Socorro de Rio Branco nessa quinta-feira (3) e o objeto foi retirado na manhã desta sexta (4) por meio de uma endoscopia.
articles.body:
Uma criança de 1 ano e 9 meses deu entrada no Pronto-Socorro de Rio Branco, nessa quinta-feira (3), depois de engolir uma bateria de lítio. Com exame de imagens, os médicos encontraram o objeto dentro do estômago do menino e fizeram a retirada nesta sexta (4).

A reportagem não conseguiu contato com a família do menino. A bateria do tipo botão tem o tamanho aproximado de uma moeda, usada em brinquedos, por exemplo. Em alguns casos, é necessário realizar procedimentos como endoscopia e cirurgia para retirar o objeto.

Nesse caso, o médico Fernando Guerra indicou a retirada do objeto em caráter de urgência por meio de uma endoscopia. Conforme a Secretaria de Saúde do Acre (Sesacre), a criança permanece internada em observação nesta sexta (4) e deve receber alta neste sábado (5).

"Considerando a idade da criança, o tempo transcorrido desde a ingestão, indicamos a retirada em conjunto com a pediatria, solicitamos vaga para fazer o procedimento no centro cirúrgico. A bateria foi localizada na grande curvatura do estômago e retirada integralmente, sem intercorrências", destacou.

Bateria de lítio tipo botão estava no estômago de um menino de 1 ano e 9 meses — Foto: Reprodução

Ainda segundo o profissional, não havia úlceras, sangramentos e nem sinais de perfurações intestinais. O médico afirmou também que, nesses casos, a criança deve ser levada imediatamente para o hospital por conta dos riscos.

"Quando a bateria fica presa no esôfago pode produzir queimaduras graves. Pode fazer isso em poucas horas com isso de necrose, perfurações e até lesões de vias respiratórias. Pode formar fístula, hemorragias graves e até mesmo o óbito", relatou.

O profissional orienta que os pais e responsáveis não devem provocar vômitos, não aguardar o surgimento de sintomas e procurar uma unidade de saúde mais próximo o mais rápido possível.

O médico contou que a família estava em comércio quando a criança colocou a bateria na boca. Ao ver, a mãe tentou tirar, mas a criança se assustou e acabou engolindo. Eles deram entrada no pronto-socorro por volta das 20h30 dessa quinta.

"Como prevenção, baterias, além de aparelhos que utilizem baterias, devem ser deixados em compartimentos fechados com alguma trava de segurança ou parafusos", concluiu.

articles.title: Julia Louis-Dreyfus says there was a ‘ton’ of friction on the “Seinfeld” set: ‘You’re gonna butt heads’
articles.summary: “It’s hard to do anything really well and it takes a lot of work and you’re gonna butt heads,” the Emmy winner explained.
articles.body:
Julia Louis-Dreyfus is looking back at "friction" on the Seinfeld set.

The Emmy winner, who starred as Elaine, revealed there was "tons" of conflict on set during the hit comedy's run.

"It's hard to do anything really well and it takes a lot of work and you're gonna butt heads," she said.

Even a show about nothing can be stressful sometimes.

During a recent visit to the Friends Keep Secrets podcast, Emmy-winning actress Julia Louis-Dreyfus was asked if she ever experienced any "friction" on set while starring as Elaine Benes on the beloved comedy series, Seinfeld .

"Of course, yes, tons," Louis-Dreyfus replied. "I mean, it's hard to do anything really well and it takes a lot of work and you're gonna butt heads."

Created by Jerry Seinfeld and Larry David , Seinfeld followed a group of friends as they lived, worked, and found themselves in bonkers situations in New York City. In addition to Seinfeld and Louis-Dreyfus as Jerry and Elaine, the series rounded out its core four cast with Jason Alexander and Michael Richards respectively playing George and Kramer.

The show, which aired for nine seasons from 1989 until 1998, is widely considered one of the most influential comedies of all time, having spawned multiple iconic moments including: "No soup for you," George's answering machine, Kramer hosting a talk show in his apartment, and Elaine's signature dance.

Fascinatingly, during the podcast visit, Louis-Dreyfus revealed that she doesn't often rewatch any of the films or movies in which she's starred, including Seinfeld .

"I don't usually watch it, but you know what's really funny, and it's really sweet? My husband does," she said of Emmy-nominated writer Brad Hall. The two married before Seinfeld ever hit the airwaves.

"Sometimes he'll be laughing and he's just watching bloopers or something of mine," she continued. "And I'm like, 'I can't believe he's watching that.' He loves it."

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

Louis-Dreyfus also recalled an instance in which the show's network, NBC, wanted to hold a major television crossover event that would've seen Seinfeld , Friends , and its other programs all navigating the same New York City blackout.

"That was the network's idea, that because that was Must-See TV back then, everybody was watching on Thursday nights," she explained to the podcasters. "And so the idea would be all the episodes have a blackout to contend with, and that's lots of fun for the audience."

While the network was excited by the idea, Louis-Dreyfus noted that Seinfeld never participated in an event like that, thanks to its co-creator. "Larry, not in a million years, would go along with anything like that," she teased.

articles.title: GoPro says it’s still committed ‘to your collective stoke’
articles.summary: GoPro CEO Nick Woodman says the company will keep making its consumer action cameras after being acquired by Starman.
articles.body: GoPro CEO Nick Woodman said in a letter to customers that making cameras is still his company’s “core DNA,” after a proposed $285 million acquisition by Starman was announced earlier this week. He claims the merger puts GoPro in a better position to continue developing its content creation tech, after saying in the deal announcement that it would work with Starman to address “important areas of national security related to cameras, optics and AI infrastructure.” YouTuber Mark “Markiplier” Fischbach, who prior to the acquisition became GoPro’s largest individual shareholder, is not mentioned at all. > To our GoPro community, fans and customers, > We understand there’s some concern about GoPro’s post-merger commitment to continue developing market leading cameras for consumers and professionals. Making amazing cameras for all of you is our core DNA and reason for being and that will never change! We’re fired up about what’s ahead for GoPro and want to share a little more about what our proposed merger with Starman means for our future. > Thanks to the improved financial strength this merger will provide, we’ll be in a much better position to innovate, invent and advance the future of consumer and professional content creation. And importantly, Starman shares our passion for the GoPro brand, developing market leading products and our commitment to your collective stoke. > We’ve accumulated more than 2500 patents over the last 24 years which tells you we’ve been busy innovating, and this merger will ensure we’re able to innovate for many more years to come. We expect this merger will make GoPro a stronger, more capable camera company than ever before. > Our goal is to become a more diversified company which can make us stronger financially, enabling GoPro to become as awesome as we (and you) want us to be. We plan to bring you more innovative cameras, smarter accessories, and more powerful software and services designed to make capturing, editing and sharing your experiences easier and more exciting than ever. We see opportunities to improve the products you already love while developing new tools and experiences that help you create, connect and share in entirely new ways. > We have so much more to do, so much more to invent, and so much more we want to bring to the GoPro community. We appreciate all of you who have been on this journey with us and we’re excited about where we’re headed. We’re going to keep doing what we do best - making the world’s highest-performance cameras and building the products, services and innovations that help you capture life’s most exciting moments. It’s what we were founded to do and it’s what we will always do. Be a HERO…GoPro. > With respect and appreciation — Nick > GoPro Founder & CEO

articles.title: ‘Wheel of Fortune’ Announcer Jim Thornton Fired After Sony Investigation
articles.summary: The performer was interrogated by police after troubling chat room activity during a flight
articles.body:
"Wheel of Fortune" announcer Jim Thornton was fired by Sony after an investigation, following a mid-flight incident in May .

The performer was interrogated by police after his behavior during a flight was flagged by another passenger. TMZ, who first reported Thornton's initial suspension, later shared screenshots of troubling chat room activity captured by the passenger .

"Following a thorough investigation, Jim Thornton's employment with 'Wheel of Fortune' has been terminated, effectively immediately," the studio said in a statement to media.

Thornton's termination comes just three days after he was suspended by Sony Pictures Television, which followed the initial report from TMZ that an incident occurred on a commercial plane that was escalated from a complaint from a passenger to a flight attendent.

"We have recently been made aware of allegations concerning Jim Thornton," a Sony Pictures TV spokesperson said in a statement at the time. "He has been suspended from 'Wheel of Fortune' and we are recasting while we conduct a thorough investigation."

The company did not provide details regarding the allegations, but the incident eventually made it up the chain high enough for the pilot to call ahead to law enforcement to have them meet Thornton at the gate. He was questioned before being released from law enforcement.

"On May 14, American Airlines Flight 1276 was met by law enforcement upon arrival at Los Angeles International Airport following concerns reported by a customer onboard," American Airlines said in a statement to media.

The announcer's lawyer told TMZ Wednesday he "did not engage in any illegal conduct, was not arrested and has not been charged with any crime."

"When questioned about the complaint made by a fellow passenger on the flight, law enforcement spoke to him for five minutes or less, immediately determined that no wrongdoing had occurred and told my client he was free to go," the attorney continued.

articles.title: The weird and wonderful headphones of CanJam 2026
articles.summary: ﻿Mainstream headphones are good but boring now. I went to an audiophile show to be reminded why I love headphones.
articles.body: I’ve been reviewing headphones for a long time, and I’ve listened to everything from the barely serviceable to multi-thousand-dollar open-back headphones. But recently I’ve been uninspired by the state of mainstream options. Most are perfectly good — great, even — but they lack a distinct character. Something to remind me why I fell in love with headphones to begin with, landing me in this crazy career. I needed some revitalization. I needed to see something cool. I needed to be around other people with an emotional connection to headphones. I needed to go to CanJam. CanJam is a small audio show produced by Head-Fi.org, the largest audio-focused online forum, with multiple events a year at different places around the world, including London, Shanghai, New York City, Dubai, and Southern California. It’s where mainly boutique manufacturers exhibit their latest headphones and related gear to enthusiasts constantly searching for the most accurate and engaging audio experience they can find. You won’t find Bose or Apple here — although Sony’s Pro division was there, as were some familiar names like Sennheiser and Audeze. In all my years covering A/V gear, I’ve never actually made it to a CanJam. Either it wasn’t an interest for the outlets I was writing for, or personal obligations kept me from going. But this year, my first at The Verge, felt like the right time. So on August 29th, I braved the 405 from Los Angeles down to Irvine, California. CanJam SoCal 2026 was in a convention space at the Irvine Marriott. Most exhibitors — including larger audio names like Sennheiser, Focal, and HiFiMan as well as niche brands like Astell&Kern and Noble Audio — had booths in the biggest room. Many set up listening stations with tablets running Qobuz (the streaming service of choice for audiophiles because of its hi-res lossless audio) to demonstrate their headphones, DACs, amps, media players, and even cables. Others were in quieter rooms off the main hallway, more conducive to listening. And crowding into those rooms and booths were a couple thousand audio enthusiasts. [Image: The Chimera look gorgeous, but are bigger than most other in-ears. My first stop was the Campfire Audio booth. Campfire Audio builds earbuds in Portland, Oregon; I’ve listened to its $1,500 Solaris and $300 IO in-ear monitors in the past. Today, though, was for an in-ear monitor that debuted at CanJam Singapore in May: the Campfire Audio Chimera. Most mainstream earbuds and headphones have a single driver per ear that has to reproduce every frequency from the lowest bass to the highest treble. Two if you’re lucky. The Chimeras have nine. It’s a “quad-brid” design, meaning they use four different types of audio delivery in a single IEM: a dynamic driver for bass and lower mids; a dual-diaphragm balanced armature (BA) for midrange clarity and two more for the high end; four electrostatic tweeters to add high-end air and spaciousness; and bone conduction for extra bass. Because of the number of drivers, the Chimera are chonky: about the size of a piece of Bubblicious bubble gum. It took some finagling to get them comfortably in place. Once I did, though, I was immediately impressed. The low end was nice and full, without getting muddy or overpowering the frequencies above. An open high end gave space to allow cymbals to shimmer and decay while avoiding any abrasiveness. The real star, though, was the midrange. Both the quiet, conversational passages of Tracy Chapman and passionate wailing of Janis Joplin sounded as if they were right there in front of me. Even though I was listening while standing in a conference hall, the Chimera delivered one of the most detailed and enjoyable listening sessions I’ve had in a long time. But they’re also $7,500. That pricing isn’t unheard of in the audiophile world — boutique, hand-built audio gear is always more expensive — but the Chimera are at another level, even compared to the rest of Campfire’s lineup. In addition to the design and engineering necessary to create a small(ish) in-ear with nine drivers all working together, much of that price is also because of materials and manufacturing. They have a carbon fiber and brass Damascus construction, with folded layers that create a topographical map design. And because of that process, the slight variations in finish make each Chimera unique. They also have a six-conductor cable that by itself is more expensive than most people’s earbuds, and include a microfiber cloth, IEM cleaning tool, and nine different tip options. [Image: Planar magnetic headphones are big, but the detail they provide is incredible. Not every product at CanJam is that far out of reach, though. Fosi Audio had wired in-ears for under $150 that sounded good for the price, plus an interesting portable CD player. The Dan Clark Audio Aeon Core planar magnetic headphones — which aren’t cheap at $900, but still more accessible than the Chimera — had a nice, wide soundstage, where the background vocals in the Black Crowes’ “Remedy” wrapped around to sing from my left and right, with Chris Robinson in front. Snare hits snapped and cymbals sizzled, although on “Fast Car” by Tracy Chapman the snare verged on being too much. I’ve been a fan of Dan Clark Audio headphones since the company was MrSpeakers, and I could easily envision myself relaxing on the couch with the Aeon Core. The Aeon Core are closed-back headphones, so it was easy to concentrate on the music even with the bustle around me. But many audiophile headphones are open-back, and a busy show floor is not an ideal space for getting a good impression. I tried a pair of $1,449 HiFiMan Arya headphones with an onboard Wi-Fi receiver. Wi-Fi is still rare in headphones (although the recently announced Sonos Ace Ultras have it); it’s better at streaming lossless audio over longer ranges than Bluetooth. They sounded good, but with their open-back planar design it’s difficult to get a strong opinion. [Image: These headphones have that nice vacuum-tube glow. On my last loop of the show floor to see if there was anything I missed, a glowing ear cup caught my eye. It was a vacuum tube. In a pair of headphones! The Écoute TH2, which were funded on Kickstarter last March, are supposed to replicate a high-end two-channel audio system, all in the headphones themselves. They have a built-in vacuum tube preamp with a 6P1 tube and dual-mono amplification (the left and right channels are driven independently from the DAC to each driver). They also have solid ANC (a show floor is great for testing that) and an 8-band EQ, and they’re really comfortable. On a live recording of “A Pirate Looks at Forty” with Dave Matthews, Jack Johnson, and Tim Reynolds, I felt the audience around me as if I was at the show. There’s a lot of high-end detail, but the upper frequencies are boosted too much for my taste (I didn’t get a chance to try and tone it down with the EQ). Still, the TH2 are an incredibly interesting pair of headphones. And they are what’s great about a show like CanJam. I never would have known about the Écoute otherwise; there are so many headphones out there and only one me. Decades ago, CES used to be more about audio than robots, but there’s no going back where that’s concerned. It’s all the more reason why CanJam and shows like it need to stick around.

articles.title: Oura is going public, but these smart ring companies are coming for its crown | TechCrunch
articles.summary: While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, a growing number of rivals are now racing to dethrone it by trying all sorts of approaches to get an edge over it.
articles.body:
The smart ring market is getting crowded, and Oura isn’t waiting around to see what happens next: it officially filed to go public on September 3 . The Finnish company’s revenue nearly doubled to $1.21 billion for the nine months ended June 30.

And the company is killing it right now. The Finnish company’s revenue nearly doubled to $1.21 billion for the nine months ended June 30. Oura said it sold 3.6 million rings over the past year, and that it has around 5 million paid members. The company’s move to go public follows the recent launch of the Oura Ring 5, its slimmest and lightest ring yet.

But while Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals are emerging from all corners to dethrone it, each betting on a different angle. For example, French company Circular announced this week that its upcoming ring will allow users to tap to pay with their ring, while Chinese company RingConn debuted a ring this year that added haptic vibrations.

Indian company Ultrahuman separately announced this week that it raised $70 million with backing from Qualcomm’s venture arm as it looks to build a ring that it says will be able to run software directly on the device and eventually power everything from AI interactions to games.

The race to beat Oura isn’t just about enhanced health and sleep tracking anymore. It’s now about seeing which company can cram the most smartphone-like features into a two-gram titanium band before someone ends up shipping a ring that lets you doomscroll TikTok or answer calls or do your taxes on. I mean, we’re already seeing smart rings with screens, like the Pebble Halo , although it’s currently only available in India, as well as rings that promise touchpads, like the Dreame Ring .

The irony is that the initial appeal with smart rings was that they made technology and health tracking feel less intrusive than devices like smartwatches and smartphones, given you can step away from a screen while still keeping tabs on your health. With the way things are headed in the smart ring industry, though, we may just end up slipping mini smartphones down our fingers.

All of this is to say that the smart ring market is getting increasingly confusing, so we’ve rounded up the most notable contenders vying for Oura’s crown.

Earlier this year, Ultrahuman unveiled its third-generation smart ring, the $479 Ring Pro , which is set to begin shipping in the U.S. in mid-September. Ultrahuman’s U.S. business was disrupted in October 2025 after the U.S. International Trade Commission ruled in Oura’s favor in a patent dispute. The ruling prevented the company from importing new ring inventory into the country, so Ultrahuman developed the Ring Pro with a redesigned form factor in order to circumvent Oura’s patent.

The Ring Pro features a redesigned heart-rate sensing system aimed at improving signal quality during sleep, along with a new dual-core processor that enables more accurate data collection and greater on-device processing. As noted earlier, Ultrahuman looks to be more ambitious with future rings as it aims to go beyond sleep and health tracking.

Circular’s upcoming Ring 3 series , which consists of a Pro model and a Slim option, is expected to launch early next year. Both of the smart rings will feature an integrated NFC chip for contactless payments and on-finger vibrations that can be used for silent wake-up alarms, reminders, vital health alerts, and more.

The Ring 3 Pro features a slimmer design than its predecessor and comes with FDA-cleared ECG for AFib detection, blood pressure trend tracking, glucose tracking, advanced sleep analysis, and comprehensive biometric monitoring.

Pricing for the upcoming rings is not yet available.

The RingConn Gen 3, which launched in May and starts at $349, features vascular health insights that use sensor data from the ring to assess changes in vascular strain over time after calibration with externally measured blood pressure values.

It also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, sleep, activity, and stress, among other metrics. Additionally, it features vibration alerts for health changes, sedentary reminders, and low battery. Unlike Circular, which leans on haptics to make its ring more communicative, RingConn mostly sticks to vibration as a health-alert mechanism.

Samsung became the first major tech giant to launch a smart ring in 2024. The Galaxy Ring , which costs $399, is arguably the strongest contender for anyone already invested in Samsung’s ecosystem of devices.

Compared with other smart rings on the market, the Galaxy Ring is relatively basic when it comes to advanced health and sleep tracking. It lacks features such as sleep apnea detection, which are offered by RingConn, Oura, and Ultrahuman, as well as AFib detection, which is available on Circular and RingConn smart rings.

Dreame, a relatively new entrant to the smart ring market, unveiled a ring earlier this year with haptic alerts for alarms, calls, messages, and more, along with a small touchpad that lets you do things like skip a song or snap a photo on your phone. It’s also said to offer heart rate tracking, blood oxygen monitoring, heart rate variability insights, sleep analysis, and more.

Pricing and availability have yet to be announced.

articles.title: Egyptian TV Presenter Sentenced to Death in Massive Drug Case
articles.summary: Egyptian TV host Sarah Khalifa and eleven other defendants were sentenced to death by hanging on Saturday for manufacturing and trafficking drugs. The ruling...
articles.body:
Egyptian TV host Sarah Khalifa and eleven others were sentenced to death for manufacturing and trafficking drugs, closing a high-profile criminal trial.

The defendants were found guilty of establishing a criminal gang that supplied raw materials for synthetic drugs, possessing illegal weapons, and distributing drugs.

Sarah Khalifa, known for hosting "Mission Impossible", was detained in 2025 on drug-related charges and sentenced to five years in another case involving kidnapping and assault.

Egyptian TV host Sarah Khalifa and eleven other defendants were sentenced to death by hanging on Saturday for manufacturing and trafficking drugs. The ruling closes one of Egypt's most-followed criminal trials.

The Cairo Criminal Court, which holds sessions at Fifth Settlement district, ruled that the defendants established a criminal gang that supplied the raw material for the manufacture of the synthetic drugs and distributed them. In addition, they were convicted of possessing and carrying guns and ammunition illegally, according to the state-run daily Al Ahram.

Initially, the case had twenty-eight defendants, which the local press called the 'Grand Drug Case'. Gulf News reported that nine defendants received life sentences, while seven were acquitted.

Sarah Khalifa, 39, gained fame as a presenter of "Mission Impossible", a program focused on crime and security. In addition, she owns a plastic surgery clinic and an events organization firm, according to Arab News.

It was stated in the prosecution's statement that the group divided their tasks, where some of them smuggled chemicals from abroad, others manufactured the drugs, while others distributed them, according to Akhbar Al Youm.

Over 750 kilograms (1,650 pounds) of drugs and chemicals used to manufacture them were discovered, in addition to two apartments that were used as drug manufacturing facilities. Unlicensed weapons and ammunition were discovered, according to Al Ahram.

Before pronouncing the ruling, the trial's death penalty cases were sent to the Grand Mufti of Egypt to obtain his religious opinion, Egypt Independent said. Although it is not mandatory in the process of pronouncing the death penalty sentence in Egypt, the Mufti's opinion is only advisory.

Khalifa was detained in April 2025 on suspicion of manufacturing and trafficking drugs. Authorities froze her and other co-defendants' assets. Sarah Khalifa has more than three million followers on Instagram, The New Arab said.

In another case, the same Cairo Criminal Court sentenced Sarah Khalifa and the co-defendants to five years' imprisonment for kidnapping and beating up a young man.

In Egypt, the death penalty is applicable for premeditated murder, terrorism, some cases of rape, and drug trafficking. In 2025, Egyptian courts issued 541 death sentences, according to the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms.

articles.title: Psychology says the people who check their phones constantly  not actually be bored but may be trying to escape their own thoughts and fears
articles.summary: You are waiting for a lift and, almost without thinking, your hand reaches for your phone. You are sitting in a car and there is a two-minute pause be.
articles.body: You are waiting for a lift and, almost without thinking, your hand reaches for your phone. You are sitting in a car and there is a two-minute pause before you need to get out, so you unlock the screen. You are standing in a queue, waiting for your coffee or food, and suddenly you are scrolling through messages or social media. Often, there is nothing particularly important waiting for you. You may have checked your phone only a few minutes earlier, yet the moment there is nothing else demanding your attention, the urge to look at the screen returns.Most of us would describe this as boredom. But psychology suggests that the story may be more complicated. The urge to reach for a phone during a quiet moment can sometimes be connected to our discomfort with unstructured time, mind-wandering, anxiety, uncertainty or simply the desire for immediate stimulation. In some situations, the phone may provide an easy way of interrupting thoughts before we have even become aware of what we are thinking about. This does not mean that every instance of checking a phone is an attempt to escape one's thoughts. Smartphone use is often perfectly purposeful and harmless. However, research into boredom, mind-wandering and mobile-phone behaviour raises an interesting question: what happens inside our minds when there is suddenly nothing to occupy them?One of the most widely discussed experiments on this subject was published in the journal Science in 2014 under the title“Just think: The challenges of the disengaged mind.” Researchers conducted 11 experiments in which participants were asked to spend periods of time alone with their thoughts, without the usual external entertainment or distractions. The researchers found that many participants found the experience surprisingly difficult and did not enjoy it as much as having something external to occupy their attention. In one particularly memorable experiment, participants were given the option of administering mild electric shocks to themselves while sitting alone with their thoughts, and some chose to do so rather than remain without external stimulation. The study became famous because it suggested that simply being alone with one's thoughts can be challenging for human beings. However, it is important not to exaggerate its conclusions. A later commentary questioned whether the original research had overstated the unpleasantness of thinking, pointing out that participants' experiences were not uniformly negative. The more useful conclusion is therefore not that people hate their thoughts, but that unstructured mental space can sometimes be uncomfortable or difficult to sustain.The modern smartphone changes the equation because it provides almost instant access to stimulation whenever that discomfort appears. There is no need to wait for a television programme, open a book or find another person to talk to. A phone can immediately provide a message, photograph, video, headline, search result or social-media update. That makes it remarkably efficient at filling tiny gaps in our day. The very moments that once allowed the mind to wander can now be occupied almost automatically.Research has begun examining what happens when people resist that impulse. A study titled “Psychological and physiological effects of applying self-control to the mobile phone,” published in PLOS One and indexed in PubMed, compared participants who used their phones with participants who sat without their phones and participants who had their phones available but resisted using them. The researchers found differences in concentration and mind-wandering across the conditions, although the results did not support the simple idea that being without a phone automatically makes people more bored or unhappy. This is an important distinction because it suggests that the psychological effect of putting down the phone may have more to do with attention and mental activity than with a straightforward increase in boredom.That mental activity is important because a quiet moment is rarely an empty moment for the brain. When there is no immediate task competing for attention, the mind naturally wanders. You may suddenly remember something someone said to you yesterday, think about a conversation that did not go the way you wanted, begin planning tomorrow, replay an old memory or start worrying about something that needs to be done. You might also daydream, make a creative connection or simply notice how you are feeling. Mind-wandering is a normal feature of everyday cognition, and research suggests that people spend a substantial proportion of their waking lives in this state.A systematic review and meta-analysis titled“Ecological momentary assessment of mind-wandering: meta-analysis and systematic review,” which is indexed in PubMed, examined research measuring mind-wandering in people's everyday lives. The review found that mind-wandering is common, although estimates vary considerably depending on how it is measured and the circumstances in which it occurs. This matters for smartphone behaviour because the device can become an extremely convenient interruption whenever the mind begins to wander. Instead of allowing a thought to develop, we can immediately shift our attention towards something external.Boredom, however, remains an important part of the explanation. Researchers have found associations between boredom proneness and problematic mobile-phone use. A study titled “Are bored minds more likely to be addicted? The relationship between boredom proneness and problematic mobile phone use,” published in Addictive Behaviors and indexed in PubMed, examined 1,099 college students and found that boredom proneness was associated with problematic mobile-phone use. The study also examined depression and attentional control as factors involved in the relationship. The findings suggest that boredom can contribute to excessive phone use, but they also show why it is too simplistic to say that people simply pick up their phones because they have nothing to do.Sometimes boredom itself may be an uncomfortable psychological state. When there is nothing happening externally, a person may become more aware of internal thoughts and feelings. Someone who is restless may seek stimulation. Someone who feels lonely may look for social interaction online. Someone who is worried may seek information. Someone who is simply accustomed to constant stimulation may find an unstimulated environment strangely difficult. The same physical behaviour - unlocking a phone - can therefore have very different psychological reasons behind it.Loneliness and self-control have also been investigated in relation to problematic phone use. Research titled “Loneliness and Mobile Phone Addiction Among Chinese College Students: The Mediating Roles of Boredom Proneness and Self-Control,” indexed in PubMed, examined more than 1,000 college students. The researchers found relationships between loneliness, boredom proneness and problematic mobile-phone use, with boredom and self-control playing important roles in the relationship. Again, this does not mean that checking a phone is evidence of loneliness or addiction. It suggests instead that our emotional state can influence the way we use a device that is almost always available.There is another reason people may repeatedly check their phones: uncertainty. Sometimes the motivation is not entertainment but reassurance. Did someone reply to the message? Has an email arrived? Did something happen while I was away? Is there news I should know about? Research into intolerance of uncertainty and increasing connectivity has examined how mobile technology can provide immediate access to information and reassurance. A study titled “Increasing intolerance of uncertainty over time: the potential influence of increasing connectivity,” indexed in PubMed, discussed how constant connectivity can interact with uncertainty and reassurance-seeking behaviour. In some circumstances, checking can temporarily reduce uncertainty, but repeated reassurance-seeking can also become part of a cycle that keeps the underlying anxiety alive.Habit is another piece of the puzzle. We do not always consciously decide to check our phones. The behaviour can become associated with particular situations: sitting down, waiting, waking up, going to bed or experiencing a pause in conversation. Over time, the cue itself may trigger the behaviour. The interesting part is that the person may not even know why they are reaching for the phone. The action can occur before conscious reasoning catches up.Research on craving, self-control and problematic mobile-phone use has also explored this process. A PubMed-indexed study titled “Weak and interfered self-control fails to block problematic mobile phone use: The role of craving and desire thinking” examined adolescents and found relationships between self-control, craving and problematic phone use. Such findings help explain why knowing that you have no real reason to check your phone does not necessarily eliminate the urge to do so.But there is an important reason not to turn this into another story about smartphones being inherently harmful. Smartphone use can also be enjoyable, socially meaningful and useful. A recent study titled “Investigating the Effects of Smartphone Use During Short Breaks on Cognitive Performance and Affective States,” indexed in PubMed, found that participants reported more positive mood after smartphone breaks than after sitting quietly, while the researchers did not find significant differences in subsequent cognitive performance or mind-wandering. In other words, using your phone during a break is not automatically psychologically damaging.The more interesting question, therefore, is not whether phones are good or bad. It is whether we have become so accustomed to filling every pause that we rarely notice what happens when we do not. The next time you reach for your phone while waiting for an elevator, sitting in traffic or standing in a queue, it may be worth delaying the impulse for a few seconds. Instead of immediately asking what is happening on the screen, ask yourself what was happening inside your mind immediately before you reached for it.Perhaps you were simply bored. Perhaps you were curious. Perhaps you were waiting for a message. Perhaps you were restless or anxious. Perhaps an uncomfortable thought had just surfaced. Or perhaps there was no psychological drama at all and you had simply developed a habit of filling every empty second.The distinction is important because a quiet moment is not necessarily an empty moment. Sometimes it is simply a moment in which the external world has stopped demanding your attention and your internal world gets a chance to become audible. The phone may not always be an escape from that inner world, but it is an extraordinarily efficient way of avoiding the silence long enough to find out what your mind was about to say.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: The Fairphone 6 Plus is the midrange phone we desperately needed
articles.summary: The ultra-repairable Fairphone 6 Plus isn’t just a better ethical choice for a phone; it’s actually a great device. And it’s finally available in the US.
articles.body: The Fairphone 6 Plus feels like an extremely average midrange Android phone and I couldn’t be more thrilled. The mission has always been admirable. Fairphone seeks out ethically sourced materials and offers a high degree of repairability for its devices. But the phones themselves required a lot of sacrifices, like putting up with underpowered processors and bad cameras, in order to embrace the sustainability mission. The latest generations of Fairphone have inched toward closing that gap, and the 6 Plus achieves two huge milestones: It feels very much like using a middling Android phone, and it’s actually on sale in the US. The 6 Plus is a light update to last year’s Fairphone 6, which my colleague Dominic Preston reviewed and found very easy to recommend. The 6 Plus builds on it with a newer midrange Snapdragon chipset and a new color treatment. Fairphone says it’s cobalt; we know it around these parts as blurple. Otherwise, the phone is basically the same, and the replacement parts sold by Fairphone work interchangeably with both models. But above all, this phone is just fine. It runs about as fast as your typical mid-tier Razr or A-series Pixel. It offers a pleasantly close-to-stock version of Android free of bloat or gimmicky AI features. It’s just a phone. And that’s great. [Product: Fairphone 6 Plus | I know, calling this a midrange phone when it’s priced at $649 might feel like a stretch. At best, it’s at the very top of the midrange class. But RAMageddon has done a real number on phone prices over the past year, and it’s not over yet. Given that the phone comes with 12GB of RAM, a five-year warranty, and up to six OS upgrades, that price feels more manageable. Also, you don’t need to add AppleCare or whatever to that price. You are the AppleCare. The 6 Plus has 12 user-replaceable parts including the battery, screen, USB-C port, and all three cameras. The repairs are extremely beginner-friendly — if you can use the tiny included screwdriver and follow some easy-to-parse directions, you won’t have a problem. The price of these parts compared to the cost of repairing a Google Pixel or Samsung Galaxy phone range from a pretty good deal to a hell of a good deal. Without an extended warranty of some kind, a battery replacement would typically cost in the ballpark of $100 to $180; Fairphone charges $39.99 for a new battery. A screen repair ranges from $100 to nearly $300; a new display from Fairphone costs $89.99. Add in the entirely reasonable cost of 30 minutes of your own labor (if that), and the long-term value of this phone starts looking pretty good. $649 is also a bargain compared to the $899 that the Fairphone 6 costs in the US. It was only offered preloaded with the privacy-minded /e/OS, which is a de-Googled version of Android made by a company called Murena. It’s not really for the faint of heart, and that price was pretty hard to swallow. But Fairphone is selling the 6 Plus directly in the US, with full support for T-Mobile and AT&T. I’ve had no trouble using it with my Verizon SIM for the past week, though it’s not certified on the network. [Image: More than meets the eye. Knowing how easy it is to replace parts of this phone as it ages actually required me to think a bit differently while I was using it. Battery life is just okay. I usually got through most days of light-to-moderate use with 60 percent left at bedtime. I did turn on every battery-draining feature I could think of, including the always-on display, higher screen refresh rate, and light mode. Those are all off by default, and probably for good reason. Normally I’d be pretty concerned about what that battery performance would look like in a few years. But there’s an easy fix: Just swap the battery yourself. No trip to the repair shop, no time away from your phone. Most phones would benefit from a new battery after a few years of continuous use anyway; at least with this one you can do it yourself and pay a lot less. The 6 Plus comes with way fewer compromises than early versions of the Fairphone did. The first iterations came with outdated designs, poor-quality cameras, and previous-gen displays. Things have steadily improved, but there are still some tradeoffs hanging around. The phone is rated IP55, which equates to mostly dust-resistant and mostly water-resistant, but not fully protected. Sealing up the phone completely and still offering easy repairability would be difficult, maybe impossible. That’s bad news, item one. Item two: no wireless charging, and likewise no ring of magnets a la Qi2 or MagSafe. I’m growing partial to an easily removable PopSocket on my phone, so I missed having that option here. Moving along: The screen is thoroughly decent, though it doesn’t get quite as bright in daylight as some of the nicest ones out there. The speakers are tinny. And even after more than a week with this phone, I still haven’t learned the muscle memory of finding the wake button / fingerprint scanner without looking, since it sits basically flush with the side of the phone. [Image: The wake button is a little hard to find by memory. But 10/10 for this physical slider. The Snapdragon 7S Gen 4 chipset handled the basic demands of modern life. If you poke around the edges you can find where this chipset falls short of the very best SoCs — which you can come by in devices that don’t cost much more than the Fairphone 6 Plus. Google Maps runs a little stuttery on my car’s infotainment screen when I run it with wired Android Auto, and there’s a bit of juddering as I scroll around my town in Pocket City 2. But it handles a dense webpage like Icy Veins’ character build guides remarkably well, and I can get away with a few back-to-back Portrait mode shots before the shutter button grays out to clear the buffer. Outside of very graphically intense gaming, it holds up just fine. Meeting that bar for a “decent midrange Android phone” means the Fairphone 6 Plus needs to offer a good, basic camera system. It does. It doesn’t offer one iota more than that, but it does the job. It was the camera I used to take pictures of my son’s fifth birthday, which in hindsight was a lot of trust to put into an unproven (by me at least) system. But it worked out! I have an in-focus photo of him blowing out birthday candles. That’s service journalism in action, folks. The main camera does a fine job with daylight scenes, and the app offers a 2x crop function that I used quite a bit. The ultrawide suffers some noise and smoothing in dimmer indoor light, which is pretty typical. Portrait mode is passable, and I didn’t notice any red flags in the handful of video clips I shot of my kid opening birthday presents. The camera system made some funky choices now and again, but overall I agree with Dom’s impressions of the same camera system on the preceding model: It’s fine. Not great, but certainly passable if you’re not picky. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: If that was all the Fairphone had to offer, I’d feel okay about recommending it. But there’s more, starting with the modular back panel accessories. The screwdriver included in the box is all you need to swap out the back plate and replace it with one that has a wallet or a flexible grip. There’s also a crossbody strap you can attach to any of those panels, though the jury’s still out on whether I personally can pull off a crossbody strap. This obviously isn’t as convenient as magnetic attachments, but it’s fun, and fun is hard to come by these days. The little neon-colored switch on the side of the phone is hard to miss, and it houses another one of the Fairphone’s bonus features. By default, switching it on enables something Fairphone calls “Moments,” which are basically focus modes with minimalist homescreens that limit you to a handful of apps. You can set up your own Moment modes and decide which apps you’ll have access to and who’s allowed to call you when the mode is enabled. [Image: [Image: I didn’t use this feature as much as I anticipated, mostly because I’m avoiding social media on my phone at the moment and that’s what I would most need a focus mode to keep me away from. But I think it’s a great concept and the execution appears to be sound. I’d appreciate a little more customizability, like maybe the ability to add a custom wallpaper rather than choosing from the basic options provided. But I guess the more options you add, the more room there is for distractions to wiggle in. Maybe basic really is best. Fairphone has finally created a phone that feels ready for the mainstream in the 6 and 6 Plus. It’s not just a device that represents some admirable ethical qualities — it’s a very good total package. There’s the feel-good benefit of buying from a company that, by every indication, walks the ethical and sustainability walk. But there are tangible benefits, too, like easily taking care of repairs yourself when you inevitably need them. And those upsides no longer come with such severe tradeoffs. When the price for a midrange phone seems to get higher every day, the 6 Plus starts to look like smart money. Photography by Allison Johnson / The Verge

articles.title: Let’s take a look at the retro tech making a comeback | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Boom boxes, instant cameras, and even landlines are making a comeback. Here are the coolest retro-inspired devices available.
articles.body:
From blasting music on a boom box to watching a photo develop in your hands, many people are rediscovering the imperfect charm of older gadgets that smartphones and laptops just can’t replicate.

Tech companies are leaning all the way in, blending nostalgic design with modern functionality. Here are some of the coolest retro-inspired devices out there right now.

In a world full of endless notifications, tabs, doomscrolling, and other distractions, smart typewriters are carving out a niche for a more focused writing experience. These devices strip things back to the essentials: just you, a keyboard, and your words.

Freewrite ( $699 ): Freewrite features a design inspired by classic typewriters, providing a minimalist writing experience. It includes a small screen and satisfying keys to press. However, if you need to make edits, your drafts are synced to the cloud and can be exported to any software.

Pomera ($549): A more modern take than Freewrite’s device, Pomera looks like a compact laptop and includes helpful tools like spell check, document management, and word counts. With multiple transfer options and up to 20 hours of battery life, it balances simplicity with functionality.

Boom boxes, cassette tapes, and record players

The boom box is re-emerging as both a design statement and a functional audio device. Today’s versions pair chunky buttons, cassette decks, and oversized speakers with modern upgrades like Bluetooth and rechargeable batteries. Cassette players, meanwhile, are also reappearing with enhancements, and record players continue to be popular as well.

We Are Rewind ($525): A modern reimagining of the classic boom box, the GB-001 has everything you desire in a boom box, but better. It keeps all the essential features, such as woofers, tweeters, a cassette player, and recorder, while adding Bluetooth and a rechargeable battery. With speakers delivering 104 W of power, it’s built for both nostalgia and high-quality sound.

Bumpboxx : Now live on Kickstarter, the new BB-777 is a portable boom box that has a bold ’80s aesthetic while packing in a wide range of features. It includes a powerful three-way speaker system, dual cassette decks with recording and high-speed dubbing, a built-in CD player, USB recording, and more. It also supports multiband radio, including AM and FM.

Retrospekt ($99): A minimalist take on the classic Walkman-style player, this portable cassette device features all the essentials: play, rewind, fast-forward, and record. It supports both battery power and USB-C, making it a simple but modern throwback.

Kickback World ($500): This DEKO record player started shipping in January 2025 and has become popular not just for being a step up from traditional players, but also for aesthetic appeal with its orange acrylic, “Swedish modernism” design compared to the traditional, suitcase-style record players we normally see.

There’s something uniquely satisfying about holding a physical photo seconds after taking it. That sense of excitement and anticipation, combined with the imperfect beauty of film, makes each shot feel more meaningful than a quick snap on your iPhone.

Polaroid ($249) : Polaroid has never stopped being popular, but it’s always innovating. Most recently, the Polaroid Flip launched last year, a retro-looking instant camera with modern features like autofocus and app connectivity for remote control.

Fujifilm ($225) : If you want a hybrid camera that lets you shoot digitally and print photos, then there’s the Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo . It offers the best of both worlds: instant film with the flexibility of digital storage and sharing. In recent years, the device received an upgrade with USB-C. In January, Fujifilm launched a new variant, the Instax Mini Evo Cinema ($412) , a three-in-one hybrid camera that can even print images from your smartphone.

Kodak ($30) : You also can’t go wrong with a classic single-use, disposable camera. It’s simple, reliable, and still delivers quality photos without needing any photography skills. Last year, Kodak released a miniature keychain digital camera, the “Charmera.” A twist on its signature “Fling” camera, this tiny device can save and transfer photos and videos using a USB-C cable.

Landline phones are making a quiet comeback, especially among people seeking a break from screen-heavy communication. They’re also gaining popularity as aesthetic objects, often used as statement pieces in home décor.

Tin Can ($100): Remember the days when you would rush home after school to use the landline and chat with your friends for hours? That’s the inspiration behind Tin Can. Designed for kids, it resembles a landline phone but doesn’t require a phone jack, just Wi-Fi. Only approved people can call, and parents can easily manage contacts through a companion app. There’s a free plan to call other Tin Can users and a $9.99/month plan for calling all approved contacts.

Clicks ($499): Announced at CES 2026 , hardware company Clicks Technology debuted its smartphone that looks a lot like a BlackBerry, which dominated the phone market back in the 2000s and has seen a revival among Gen Z. While Clicks’ phone has access to text messaging and productivity apps like Gmail and Slack, it doesn’t provide access to mobile games and social media, making it an enticing alternative for people looking to go back to the good old days.

Pinwheel Home ($68): In July, the kid-focused tech company launched its modern take on the landline phone, giving kids a screenless way to stay connected with family and friends. Like Tin Can, Pinwheel Home operates over Wi-Fi, and parents can approve contacts through Pinwheel’s Caregiver Portal. Calls made between Pinwheel Home devices are free. For families interested in calling regular phone numbers, there are plans starting at $6.99/month for up to five approved contacts, or $9.99/month for unlimited calling.

Ooma MyPhone ($100): Another kid-friendly home phone option that’s designed as a modern alternative to traditional landlines. It allows calls only between approved contacts and includes Quiet Hours, emergency alerts, and parental call log monitoring. There are no apps, internet access, texting, or social media. The home phone service plan costs $7.99/month.

This post originally published March 28 and has since been updated to reflected updated pricing and discounts.

articles.title: Boox’s tiny Picco e-reader should land in November
articles.summary: There won’t be magnets and there’s still no word on price, though.
articles.body: Boox teased the Picco, its take on the buzzy Xteink X4 e-reader, back in July, but provided almost no details. Now, thanks to some reporting out of IFA, we’ve got a bit more info, though sadly still no price. Unlike the Xteink devices, the Picco will not have magnets on the back for attaching to a phone. The 3.97-inch e-paper display, however, will be touchscreen, which The Verge’s Andrew Liszewski called a “welcome upgrade” on the X4 Pro. The Picco has physical page-turn buttons, and they can be customized with different actions for short and long presses. There’s apparently no onboard storage, and it relies entirely on a microSD card to hold books. But in addition to adding files to the card, you can transfer reading material to the Picco directly over USB-C (which the Xteink devices lack) or even WiFi from a companion app. The Picco won’t run Android, like Boox’s other devices, and will instead run a stripped-down, Linux-based OS. The company is including a handful of additional apps like a timer, a todo list, and a reading stats tracker. But, it’s unlikely that Boox will open its firmware like Xteink has, so it might be a less hackable and customizable device. There’s still some things we don’t know, like price, battery life, Bluetooth support, or if it will include a player for audiobooks. But all should be revealed in November, when it’s expected to launch.
